about: Songs, not clips. Each song has versions (one Suno generation each, oldest first), and each version has two takes (Suno makes two per generation). stage is the song's maturity: idea, experiment, shortlist, pre-release, released. pick is the take chosen to carry the song forward (null until chosen). To make this site your own, fork the repository and replace these songs with your own public Suno songs.

stages.about: Lyrics and a style, not yet generated.
Versions being tried; nothing chosen yet.
One take picked to carry the song forward, with your votes in mind.
The picked take downloaded at full quality, with title, lyrics and cover, ready to release.

source: Read from the team's Suno library through Suno's MCP connection by suno.b@SovereignWebsite.dinis, 23 November 2026. Takes are paired by the generation they came from (same creation time). Version labels are short descriptions of each prompt.

songs.title: Parada
songs.about: An instrumental with a Brazilian feel: a strong melody carried by instruments, and hard stops and starts. Parada is Portuguese for stop.

brief.asked_by: Dinis Cruz, 23 November 2026, in suno.b's session
brief.words: When you create a song that has a very sort of Brazilian feel with a very strong melody, kind of a bit like the TikTok songs [read as: Tick Tock, Nineteen Hours], the last ones, they're really cool, but purely instrumental, no melody [read as: no singing], but with really nice stops and starts and really good. I'd like you to explore how much we can do in terms of instrument kind of melodic lines in there.
thinking: Start from what Dinis liked in Tick Tock's last version: samba batucada, cavaquinho, a bright 118 to 120 bpm pulse.
Take the voice out (instrumental on, and vocals, choir, humming and spoken words in the styles to avoid), so the melody has to live in the instruments.
Name who carries the tune: cavaquinho and flute in unison for the theme, nylon guitar and muted trumpet answering, so there is call and response without a singer.
Ask for the stops in words Suno tends to follow: tight full-band stops and breaks, sudden silences, the band crashing back in.
Two minutes, so the stops have room but the idea stays tight.
brief.versions_note: Version 2 has its own brief (below the prompt).

versions.result: Both takes are fully instrumental with a strong melody and four or five full-band stops. Neither used the cavaquinho and flute asked for: take A went to horns (trumpet, clarinet, trombone), take B to an accordion-like reed and plucked guitar. Next version: ask for less reinterpretation (variety 0, style influence high) and name the instruments again, or keep the horns if they work.

versions.label: Slower and jazzier, built on version 1 take A

prompt.mode: simple, instrumental, built on Parada version 1 take A (reference)
prompt.style: A slower version of Parada, around 92 bpm, keeping its main melodic line on the horns and its full-band stops, and keeping the samba batucada percussion (surdo, pandeiro, tamborim) but laid back. Move it towards sophisticated Brazilian jazz and MPB: warm nylon-string guitar with rich jazz chords, smooth fretless bass, soft Rhodes, gentle syncopated groove, a relaxed and sunny late-afternoon feel. Purely instrumental, no vocals.
prompt.suno_expanded: Sophisticated Brazilian jazz and MPB, relaxed samba batucada around 92 BPM, preserve the source's catchy main horn melody and dramatic full-band stops with sudden silences and strong ensemble returns. Warm nylon-string guitar playing rich extended jazz chords, smooth fretless bass, soft Rhodes, laid-back syncopated surdo, pandeiro and tamborim, understated agogo accents. Sunny late-afternoon ease, supple dynamics, warm organic ensemble sound, clear melodic horns up front, polished spacious mix.

versions.style: slower Brazilian jazz and MPB, relaxed batucada, melody kept, instrumental

brief.asked_by: Dinis Cruz, 24 November 2026, in suno.b's session
brief.words: So for the next song, can you do a variation of this, much slower, a bit slower, but still keep the battocada, but do a bit slower, and try to do a little bit like a kind of sort of DJava [read as: Djavan], kind of Gilberto Gil style, with what's it called Brazilian Jazz? With keeping the sort of melodic line, which I really like, and it's really cool.
thinking: Build on the take Dinis had loaded (version 1, take A) so the melodic line carries over: Suno's reference mode.
Suno does not take artists' names, so describe the sound instead: Brazilian jazz and MPB, nylon guitar with rich jazz chords, fretless bass, Rhodes, a late-afternoon feel.
Keep the batucada but laid back; ask for about 92 bpm.

listen.summary: Bright flute-like lead with piano and brass answering; relaxed batucada and jazz-coloured chords; no full-band silences, only short accents.

stops: brief full-band break before the closing chord
listen.summary: Warm flute lead with saxophone answering and light piano; soft batucada and bossa-MPB jazz harmony; one clear break near the end.

versions.result: Half there. The batucada stayed, now relaxed; the harmony moved to Brazilian jazz and MPB with richer chords; the melody is still strong (4 of 5), now on flute with piano, brass or saxophone answering; still instrumental. But it is not slower: both takes measure 120 bpm, as in version 1 (building on the original kept its tempo), and the hard stops are mostly gone (none in take A, one near the end of take B). Next: write the style ourselves at about 88 bpm with half-time feel and the stops named, without building on the original. Suno titled these takes Luz de Tarde.
